text: Chapter four is about not retyping the same journal every month. A monthly rent allocation, a flat intercompany charge — define it once, and let General Ledger generate it each period instead. There are three ways to define one.

Skeleton journals keep the same accounts every period, but you type in this period's amount by hand after generating. Standard journals keep the same accounts and the same amount every single time — nothing to type at all. Formula journals keep the same accounts, but calculate the amount from a formula, so no one types anything, yet the number can still change.

Here's what a formula can actually pull from. Fixed constants, account balances — standard, end-of-day, or average — actual or budget amounts, statistics like headcount or square footage, and period-to-date or year-to-date balances from the current period, the prior period, or the same period last year. For example, a fictional IT cost allocation could calculate a department's share by multiplying its headcount ratio against the IT department's actual expense for the period — pulled straight from the ledger, never typed by hand.

So which type fits which situation? Standard, when the amount genuinely never changes. Skeleton, when the accounts are fixed but you still want a human to confirm this period's number before it posts. Formula, when the amount is derivable from data already sitting in the ledger.
Defining the journal is only half the story — it still has to actually get generated each period. That's lesson eighteen: generating recurring journals.
